query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled cold-working (plastic deformation) pre-treatment to the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating prior to sliding wear testing will significantly enhance its wear resistance across a wide temperature range by increasing defect density to accelerate the formation of a protective, Cr-rich oxide scale, thereby shifting the wear mechanism from abrasive/oxidative removal to protective passivation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, in an as-deposited or as-sintered state with low dislocation density and no pre-existing protective oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled cold-working process (e.g., shot peening or surface rolling) to the coating surface to introduce a high density of crystal defects and dislocations.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear conditions spanning temperatures from ambient to elevated levels (e.g., 200°C–600°C), varying friction velocities, and varying wear depths, in an oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: High density of crystal defects (dislocations, vacancies) and increased grain boundary area created by cold working, which act as fast diffusion paths for Chromium.
generation.mechanism: The cold-worked state increases the concentration of defects, which accelerates the diffusion of Chromium (Cr) from the bulk alloy to the surface during sliding and heating. This rapid Cr supply facilitates the immediate formation of a dense, adherent Cr-rich oxide layer (Cr2O3) that acts as a protective barrier, preventing the continuous formation and removal of rough, inhomogeneous oxides that cause high wear rates in the untreated state.
generation.predicted_outcome: The cold-worked FeNiCrCoCu coating will exhibit a significantly lower wear depth and a lower coefficient of friction compared to the untreated coating under identical sliding conditions, particularly at elevated temperatures where the protective oxide layer is most effective.
generation.baseline: The untreated FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical sliding conditions, which is predicted to show higher wear depth due to the formation of rough, inhomogeneous oxides that are continuously removed during sliding.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for temperatures where Cr oxidation is thermodynamically favorable (typically >300°C) and for cold-work strains that do not induce macro-cracking or delamination of the coating from the Cu matrix. It may fail if the cold-work induces excessive brittleness leading to spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.uncertainty: The specific optimal level of cold-work strain required to maximize Cr diffusion without compromising coating adhesion to the Cu matrix is unknown. Additionally, the exact kinetics of oxide formation in the specific FeNiCrCoCu system compared to the cited Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni or Cr-1Mo systems may differ, potentially altering the temperature threshold for protection.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on Cu matrices: Set A (Control) remains in the as-deposited state, while Set B (Intervention) undergoes a standardized cold-working process (e.g., 10% surface reduction). Both sets are subjected to reciprocating sliding wear tests at three temperatures (Room Temp, 400°C, 600°C) with identical load and velocity. Post-wear, cross-sectional TEM and EDS mapping are performed on the wear tracks.
measurements: Cr concentration profile in the oxide scale (EDS/EPMA)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the cold-worked samples (Set B) show no statistically significant reduction in wear depth compared to the control (Set A) at elevated temperatures, OR if the cold-worked samples exhibit a Cr-rich oxide layer that is not more continuous or protective than that of the control, OR if the cold-worked samples show increased wear due to oxide spallation caused by the induced defects.
